cards.title: Allocate 31–43% of Q4 budget to September–October pre-spend
cards.summary: Shift a large share of Q4 media budget into September and October because pre-sale spend builds the funnel that converts when the sale goes live.
cards.use_when: Planning Q4 / Black Friday budget allocation for your store and deciding how much to spend before sale week versus during it.
steps: Ignore blended October/early-November ROAS as the primary signal; it reads as the worst spend of the quarter because the funnel is being loaded, not harvested. Source frames pre-sale spend as 'causal' to Black Friday revenue.

Recalculate your CAC tolerance for pre-sale spend by adjusting for two things: lower gross margins during the sale, and historically weaker 6-month repeat purchase rates (LTV) for November-acquired cohorts versus evergreen cohorts.
Set a target to place roughly 31–43% of Q4 budget into September and October to build top-of-funnel reach before the auction inflates (source-specific heuristic, not a formula).
Build a post-treatment measurement window into any pre-season spend plan so you don't under-credit the spend that builds the Black Friday weekend.
Reconcile the final picture against the P&L, not just platform ROAS, because platform attribution is most flattering during the weekend and least flattering in the run-up.
caveats: 31–43% is the source's recommendation for its client portfolio, not a universal benchmark.
2026 context in the source: higher rates, sticky inflation, tighter ad inventory — directionally worse consumer sentiment than 2025.
The source is opinionated that underspending before the sale is a mistake; validate against your own margin and cash position.

cards.title: Read the 30-day vs 1-day click gap as a causal spending signal
cards.summary: The gap between 1-day and 30-day click attribution widens sharply in November, revealing that pre-sale spend is causal to Black Friday revenue.
cards.use_when: Interpreting your ad platform reporting in late October and early November, and deciding whether weak pre-sale ROAS is real weakness or a lagged signal.
steps: Understand the mechanic: 1-day click attributes a purchase within 24 hours of a click; 30-day click attributes within 30 days. Normally the two differ by about 40% in revenue. In November the source reports the gap widens to roughly 80%.

Do not act on 30-day click ROAS during the pre-sale run-up. The source reports a case (a nine-figure US D2C brand) where ROAS read about 1.0 on Nov 12–13 but backdated to roughly 4.0 once a wide click-through model reattributed the sales.
Treat pre-sale platform ROAS as a lagged, temporarily weak signal, not a verdict on spend quality.

Use the historical 1-day vs 7-day click gap from your own account to estimate an adjustment: build a multiplier equal to the historic lift between the two settings, then apply it to your pacing document's ROAS target.
During the period, switch the account to 7-day click (or 7-day click + 1-day engaged) and compare multiple attribution settings side-by-side rather than trusting one.
Stop scaling when marginal CM3 flattens (see separate card); use the 1-day/7-day ratio flattening as a signal that you've stopped creating demand and started harvesting bottom-of-funnel demand.
caveats: Attribution settings and their exact behavior change over time — verify current options in your ad platform's interface.
The 40%/80% and 1.0-to-4.0 figures are from the source's portfolio and one case study, not guarantees for your account.
No single attribution setting is a source of truth; the source explicitly recommends triangulating and reconciling against the P&L.

cards.title: Build a post-treatment window into pre-season spend measurement
cards.summary: Spend that runs before a sale produces measurable incremental lift after the test window ends, and this lift is much larger around Black Friday than in evergreen periods.
cards.use_when: Designing geo-holdout or incrementality experiments for your store, and deciding how long to measure after a test ends before calling it a loss.
steps: Understand post-treatment lift: after an incrementality experiment's treatment window closes and you return spend to normal, measured incremental revenue can continue to appear. Source (House) reports experiments ending 3+ weeks before Black Friday produced a 105% post-treatment lift, and close-to-Black-Friday experiments added 41% of incremental value after the treatment window.

For your own storefront: if you scale spend in a region before the sale and then pull back, do not close the experiment at the pullback date — extend the measurement window to capture delayed conversions the sale triggers.

Category context from the source: fashion/apparel showed 93% post-treatment lift; health/wellness/food/beverage (CPG) showed 30%. If you're in fashion, backfill more pre-spend than if you're in CPG (these are source-cited category figures, not universal).
Source's framing: holding back budget ahead of Black Friday is 'digging a deeper hole,' not saving dry powder — because the delayed effects are large.
Reconcile experiment conclusions against marginal, not blended, returns so you don't credit lift the experiment didn't cause.
caveats: These figures come from a specific incrementality platform's report and one presenter's portfolio; they are illustrative, not benchmarks for your category.
Incrementality tools and their measurement windows change; verify current methodology before committing budget.
Post-treatment effects can also reflect organic seasonality — the source itself flags the causal-measurement limits of observational data.

cards.title: Back-spend into the sale to avoid shrinking your own funnel
cards.summary: Underspending before a sale reduces top-of-funnel reach exactly when you need it, making the sale-conversion spike smaller.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pull back or maintain ad spend in the days before your Black Friday sale opens.
steps: Recognize the mechanism: pre-sale conversion rates dip because shoppers hold out for the known upcoming sale. Converting spend fell in the source's portfolio in early November.
Do not interpret that dip as a reason to cut spend. Cutting spend shrinks top-of-funnel awareness and traffic, so when the sale opens there's a smaller funnel to collapse into purchases.
A sale collapses the whole existing funnel — people who knew about the brand but hadn't bought — into a revenue peak, which is why every sale is followed by a slump.
Deliberately back-spend into the sale period so the funnel is bigger when it opens; the ROAS will look weak before the sale and strong during it.
Source's Q4 allocation recommendation is roughly doubling November spend relative to October while keeping meaningful September/October pre-spend — not a light warm-up plus an all-November bet.
In the source's own client data, stores spending $500K–2M in November spent ~1.76–1.8x their October spend; the source treats that as a reasonable pattern, not a rule.
caveats: The 1.76–1.8x multiplier and the 31–43% Q4 split are source-portfolio observations from specific spend brackets (November spend between $500K and $2M+).
Small brands with a smaller addressable audience may hit frequency limits faster — see the saturation card.

cards.title: Scale to marginal contribution margin (CM3), not blended ROAS
cards.summary: Averages mask the true return of the next dollar; scale spend until marginal contribution margin 3 stops improving, not until blended ROAS hits a target.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to push or pull ad spend during a peak sale weekend in your store.
steps: Stop judging spend on blended averages: source example — baseline new-customer CAC $337; adding $80K (25% more spend) degrades average CAC to $392, still below a $400 tolerance. But the marginal CAC on that $80K was $1,000, far above tolerance — the average hid an unprofitable layer.
Define your break-even ROAS as 1 / gross margin, and scale toward where marginal ROAS equals that break-even ROAS — that's where CM3 peaks.
Use CM3 as the floor, not a blended ROAS target. Keep scaling until CM3 starts to flatten; flattening means no more marginal room.
At that flattening point, you've stopped creating demand and started harvesting bottom-of-funnel demand.
Use the 1-day to 7-day click ratio as a companion check — the source watches it closely as a flattening signal.
caveats: The elasticity calculation the source uses is observational, not causal — it only gives an upper bound and can cause severe overspend if used to scale, because you naturally spend more on high-demand days. The source uses it only to cut, never to push.
The $337/$392/$1,000 example is illustrative maths, not a benchmark.

cards.title: Use revenue-spend elasticity to cut spend, never to scale it
cards.summary: A log-based elasticity score tells you if you're underspending or overextended, but it is correlation only, so use it to trim spend rather than justify more.
cards.use_when: Reviewing intraweek or intraday ad performance during a sale and deciding whether to cut spend on a channel or account.
steps: Compute elasticity as log(revenue day 2 / revenue day 1) / log(spend day 2 / spend day 1) to get a normalized figure roughly between 0 and 2 — higher suggests underspending, lower suggests overspending.
Apply a 3–4 day rolling delay to smooth noise.
Because you spend more on the days you already expect high demand, the number overstates elasticity (it captures correlation, not causation). Only use it to reduce spend, never to add.
Pair it with marginal CAC and CM3 checks before acting on any cut.
Use it as one input in a triangulation approach, alongside multiple attribution settings and the P&L.
caveats: The source is explicit that this is correlational and can cause severe overspend if misused as a scaling signal.
The 0–2 band is a rough normalization, not a validated threshold.

cards.title: Expect CPMs to spike and reach to fall during November — buy before the auction inflates
cards.summary: Auction pressure pushes CPMs up 25–50% during Black Friday, so November is a harvest period, not an acquisition period — you can only convert what you already built.
cards.use_when: Setting your media plan and reach assumptions for November and deciding when to buy audience-building impressions.
steps: Source data across ~$50–100M of ad spend: CPMs run 25–30% above October baseline starting around Nov 12, then spike higher through the weekend.

Triple Whale's 2025 Black Friday report cited in the source: Meta CPMs up ~50% period-on-period; Google up only ~10%. Meta CPA improved and ROAS improved (offsetting margin compression); Google CPA and ROAS both worsened.
Treat November as bottom/mid-funnel harvesting: you cannot meaningfully buy top-of-funnel audiences — you can only harvest what you already built.
Plan reach shortfall explicitly. If you spend the same budget at spike CPMs you reach fewer people; budget for lower reach or accept fewer impressions.
Build your top-of-funnel reach earlier (September/October) so it's available to convert when the sale opens.
Expect ad inventory growth of ~18% (2025) to compress in 2026, which makes price-per-ad increases likely — don't count on sub-2025 CPMs.
caveats: The 25–30% and 50% figures come from different source reports with different methodology, as the source itself notes. Treat as directional.
Platform pricing and inventory policies change; verify current data before locking budgets.

cards.title: Exploit the post-Christmas CPM window (Q5) with a deliberate offer
cards.summary: CPMs drop massively between Dec 16–31, making it a cheap period to roll a fresh offer into if you have the inventory and creative prepared.
cards.use_when: Planning a post-Christmas promotion or deciding whether to extend a sale into the low-competition late-December window.
steps: Reserve a December offer (bundle, gift-with-purchase, clearance) to launch after Christmas, when auction pressure falls.

Expect CPMs to be lower than Black Friday, but note they may inflate modestly if your offer performs very well — source explains CPM is correlated with expected action rate on the landing page, so Meta charges more when your store converts well.
Have creative and landing pages pre-built for this window so you can launch without delay and capture the cheap inventory.
Use this period to move any remaining Grade C or slow inventory rather than discounting it inside Black Friday.
Reconcile the window against your P&L, since a Q5 offer on clearance stock will run at lower margins.
caveats: The source calls it 'Q5' but this is jargon, not a platform-defined period.
CPM direction and magnitude vary year to year; verify current auction conditions before committing.

cards.title: Recognize that audience saturation is offer/creative fatigue, not reach exhaustion
cards.summary: Frequency barely rises during Black Friday, so declining response is usually fatigue on the offer or creative, not running out of people.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why an ad set or account stops responding mid-Black-Friday and deciding whether to rotate creative or expand audiences.
steps: Source portfolio data: baseline frequency 1.75, peaking at 1.96 during Black Friday, pulling back to 1.82 in Q5. The source says nobody really ran out of people.
When an account stops responding at peak, first check offer and creative fatigue, not audience size.
Only treat it as a reach problem if you under-spent into the period and built too small a funnel (see the funnel-flattening card).
Rotate creatives and refresh offers before broadening audiences, since the source suggests you usually have reach left.
For smaller brands, expect frequency to climb higher if you don't have a large audience pool — the source's data is from large brands.
caveats: The 1.75/1.96/1.82 figures are portfolio-level from large brands; small brands with narrow audiences may hit real reach limits.
Frequency thresholds for 'too high' differ by channel and audience — verify in your own account.
The source notes exhaustion can sometimes be an audience-reach issue if you didn't spend enough into the period.

cards.title: Model base and stretch scenarios with pre-agreed unlock thresholds
cards.summary: Enter Black Friday with two budgets and clear efficiency/spend unlock rules so spend can push up or pull back without waiting for owner approval.
cards.use_when: Setting up your Black Friday pacing plan and delegating spend authority for the peak weekend.
steps: Build a base case and a stretch case, each with explicit efficiency gates (e.g. CM3 floor, marginal CAC ceiling, ROAS band).
Define the conditions under which the team is auto-authorized to move to the stretch case — the source calls these 'pre-agreed efficiency and spend unlocks.'
Define the conditions that trigger a pullback, so cuts don't require a live check-in either.

Treat the budget as a ceiling to be deployed based on incremental returns, not a target to be spent. Source is explicit: 'The goal's not to spend the budget.' This matters most for large retailers with a mandated spend figure.
Document the stretch target as a team goal — source says it gave the team something to work toward and prevented coasting on the base case.
Keep the pacing sheet updated daily (or intraday at very high spend levels) against the unlock thresholds.
caveats: Source admits people underspend pre-sale because conversion rates dip — the unlock structure is designed to counter that tendency.
Intraday/hourly pacing is not warranted for every account; source says it's overkill for many.
Not all teams have authority to run auto-unlocks — agree in advance on who approves.

cards.title: Prepare Google Ads as a harvest platform, not a ramp platform
cards.summary: Google Ads needs structural preparation (asset, feed, and promotion updates) before Black Friday; scaling budgets in real time is usually the wrong move.
cards.use_when: Setting up Google Search, Shopping and PMax campaigns ahead of a Black Friday sale, and deciding whether to scale Google budget during the weekend.
steps: Update titles, descriptions and assets across search and PMax to be Black Friday-relevant and contextualized.
Roll over Merchant Center product feeds, set up promotion feeds, and add promotional assets and promotional titles to search and PMax.
Add discounted price lines so pricing is consistent across feeds and landing pages.
Expect these preparation steps to lift CTR and conversion rate versus competitors who skip them — the source treats this as the main Google lever, not budget pushes.

During the weekend, avoid cranking Google budget just because ROAS looks high. Source's Triple Whale citation: on Google, CPA worsened and ROAS worsened during the Black Friday weekend (period-on-period), and impression-to-purchase dropped — Google was less efficient, not more.
Source flags that Google ROAS often looks inflated because Meta traffic and branded searches are flowing in — that demand capture, not Google's own efficiency, drives the number.
Use paid incrementality checks (geo holdout) to distinguish Google-driven revenue from demand it simply captured.
caveats: Google interfaces and PMax features change; verify current asset and feed requirements before rolling over.
Triple Whale data cited is one large dataset; results vary by account.
Source's recommendation is not to eliminate Google spend, just to avoid blind budget scaling.

cards.title: Employ cost-cap campaigns during Black Friday to find the marginal frontier
cards.summary: Cost caps are avoided year-round by Blue Sense, but used during Black Friday to learn how much volume the account can absorb before diminishing returns.
cards.use_when: Testing the maximum efficient spend level in a Meta account during a high-demand sale period.
steps: Understand the source's default position: Blue Sense avoids cost caps year-round, citing account volatility and high creative volume demands.
During Black Friday, run a limited set of cost-cap campaigns alongside maximize-volume campaigns.
Observe what the cost-cap campaigns spend to — this reveals the marginal frontier the account can absorb.
Use that read to inform how aggressively to push the maximize-volume campaigns.
Do not use cost caps as the primary scaling mechanism for the whole account; they are a diagnostic tool in this context.
caveats: The source is explicitly anti-cost-cap in normal periods, so this is a Black Friday-specific tactic.
Cost-cap mechanics and performance vary by account; test before expanding.
The source calls this a portfolio-level technique, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Build an hourly-delayed attribution multiplier for intraday pacing
cards.summary: During Black Friday, spend peaks 5–7am but revenue peaks 7–11am, so early hourly ROAS must be adjusted with per-hour multipliers before you act on it.
cards.use_when: Running intraday media buying on Black Friday and interpreting early-morning ROAS to make push/pull decisions.
steps: Expect spend to peak in many accounts between 5:00 and 7:00am, while revenue peaks between 7:00 and 11:00am.
Do not compare 5am ROAS to the daily target directly — it will look artificially weak because that revenue attributes later in the day.
Build per-hour delayed attribution multipliers: the source gives an example of a 5am reading at ROAS 1 that should be treated as roughly ROAS 2 once reconciled.
Pull conversion rates by hour. The source says this has been a 'huge unlock' — it indicates ability to push spend in real time without relying on platform attribution, which lags.
Reconcile intraday spend decisions against the marginal/CM3 framework, not just hourly ROAS.
Only apply hourly pacing if spend volume is high enough to justify it — source says it's overkill for many accounts and only worth it at very high spend with rotating offers.
caveats: Hourly pacing is complex; the source warns you need to understand the delayed revenue mechanics before acting.
The 5am ROAS 1 -> ROAS 2 example is illustrative, not a fixed multiplier.
For large retailers with significant organic demand, hourly pacing may be driven by correlation rather than causation.

cards.title: Choose profit play vs inventory play before setting CAC tolerance
cards.summary: Black Friday has two distinct strategic modes — maximize contribution profit or clear slow inventory — and the answer materially changes how hard you push spend and how you KPI the weekend.
cards.use_when: Deciding your Black Friday objective for a store with slow-moving or Grade C inventory, and setting the media team's CAC and KPI thresholds.
steps: Decide in advance which play you're running: profit play (maximize contribution profit by spending to the marginal frontier) or inventory/cash play (clear slow-moving inventory at whatever discount it takes).
Discount limits are set by margin and cash/stock — source notes you can only discount a product as much as its margin allows, and the natural candidates are Grade C inventory that hasn't moved.

If you're running an inventory play, authorize the media team to accept negative incremental contribution margin at the end of the weekend to sell through stock — otherwise they'll pull back autonomously.
If you want to do both, the source suggests a gift-with-purchase bundle with multiple tiers — it moves greasy inventory (as free gifts) while still maximizing margin on the paid products.

Understand the trade-off: the source states that straight 80% off greasy inventory is a purer inventory play than bundling it as free gifts onto good (non-discounted) products — one mode will be better than the other, depending on the goal.
Tell the media team which play is in force before the weekend, because it changes both the CAC tolerance and the KPI they're managed on.
caveats: Source is explicit that you cannot do both equally well — one play will always dominate.
The gift-with-purchase structure assumes you have inventory that's genuinely slow-moving and can be bundled without cannibalizing paid product.
Cash and margin constraints, not just strategy, determine what's feasible.

cards.title: Pre-build backup offers and creative for trade-reactive Black Fridays
cards.summary: If you manage to trade/revenue targets and need to pivot offers mid-weekend, build the backup offers, landing pages, and ad creative in advance so you can switch on without production panic.
cards.use_when: Planning Black Friday operations for a store that reacts to real-time trade numbers rather than committing to one fixed offer.
steps: Identify in advance what the backup offers are — the source's examples: a gift-with-purchase, a 'TAF' (tell-a-friend / referral), free shipping, a bundle, or a deeper site-wide sale.
Build the landing pages and ad creative for each backup offer before Black Friday, and pre-load creative into ad accounts so it can be turned on instantly.
Define the trade trigger for each backup offer — the numbers that tell you to switch.
If the switch happens, redirect traffic to the new landing pages and turn on the pre-loaded creative rather than trying to edit hundreds of live assets in real time.
Accept that the pre-loaded creative may never go live — it's insurance, not waste.
caveats: The source says it is 'not super pro' on being reactive to trade, but acknowledges it if the business's revenue target requires it.
Pivoting offers across hundreds of live creatives in real time is very difficult and stressful — the whole point of pre-building is to avoid that.
Backup offer structures and ad account pre-loading capabilities may vary by platform; verify current features.

cards.title: Forecast creative volume from peak ad spend, not from a fixed creative count
cards.summary: Black Friday creative volume should be back-propagated from peak daily spend divided by realistic per-ad spend ceilings, not from a target number of assets.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many ad creatives your store needs to produce for a high-spend Black Friday.
steps: Look at last year's November data: what did your highest-spending individual ad spend per day? The source's pulled data: highest observed was ~$12.5K/day in one AUD account; most evergreen ads spent $4–8.5K; realistic working ceiling is roughly $8–13K/day.
If you want a shortcut, the source's functional estimates: average evergreen ad ~$5K/day; realistic winner ceiling ~$10–12K/day.

For your peak spend day, divide peak budget by the working per-ad ceiling to estimate how many ads you need. Example from source: $150K peak / $10–12K per ad requires 12–18 ads that can hold that spend — not 12–18 ads total.
Include a diversity buffer: the source shows that the bottom 80% of ads still hold ~54% of spend — winners alone won't carry a large account.
Distinguish clearly between 'has 12–18 ads running' and 'has 12–18 ads that can each absorb $10K/day in spend.'
caveats: The $4–12.5K per-ad figures come from the source's portfolio in AUD; your ceiling depends on your account size, offer strength and market.
The '18% of spend held by top 3 ads' and related concentration figures are portfolio data from large brands; concentration is higher for smaller accounts.
Do not treat per-ad spend ceilings as fixed limits — they are observed working ranges, not hard platform caps.

cards.title: Recognize that Pareto's principle does not apply to Black Friday creative concentration
cards.summary: Unlike evergreen periods, Black Friday spend is spread broadly across ads — the top 20% do not hold 80% of spend, so you need volume across the tail.
cards.use_when: Planning how many creatives to ship for a Black Friday campaign and whether you can rely on a small set of winners.
steps: Source finding: across the portfolio, the top single ad held ~7% of spend, top 3 held 17%, top 5 held 23%, top 10 held 33%, and top 20 held 46%. So the bottom 80% of ads still held ~54% of spend.
Abandon the assumption that the top 20% of ads will hold 80% of spend during Black Friday — it is not true across the source's portfolio.

Account size changes concentration: stores that spent under $250K in November had their top 20% of ads hold 53% of spend (then 44%, then 33% as size grew). Bigger accounts had more distribution across the tail.
Interpretation: individual ads have daily spend ceilings, so a large account naturally distributes spend more widely — plan creative volume accordingly.
Don't over-invest in perfecting the top few creatives; you need breadth because the tail does meaningful work.
caveats: These figures come from the source's portfolio of mostly large brands — smaller accounts may show higher concentration.
Concentration figures may shift year to year with platform changes and account structure.

cards.title: Use the creative format mix from last year's Black Friday portfolio as a planning reference
cards.summary: A balanced creative format mix (offer statics, overlayed evergreen, creator/founder, VSL, early access) with roughly defined spend shares held up well across a large portfolio.
cards.use_when: Deciding what types of ad creative to produce for a Black Friday campaign, and what share of spend each should hold.
steps: Source's recommended allocation: offer static ~19% of spend; offer-overlay evergreen catalog ~18%; creator/founder ads at the highest share (with founder content optional, redistributed to others if unavailable); product/VSL top-of-funnel ads at a small share; and early access/VIP ads where applicable.

Understand why each format exists: catalog evergreen showed high ROAS in the data but high frequency too — it's bottom-of-funnel retargeting, so it naturally converts well but shouldn't be over-indexed.
Offer statics are the highest-volume format — keep them 'stupid simple': discount, end date, legible at thumbnail size.
Make three variants of the same offer: vary the people in the creative, the product, or the offer itself — the source says this alone can spin out 50 statics quickly.
Test legibility by shrinking the ad: if the sale discount is unreadable at thumbnail size, redo it. Also check that 9:16 feed placements don't cut off the offer.
Put the offer or deadline in the first line of copy, because copy truncates on story and some feed placements.
No single format wins outright — the source explicitly says you need diversity of concepts, not just formats.
caveats: The 19%/18% shares are the source's recommendation from portfolio data, not validated benchmarks for your store.
Bold terminology ('stupid simple') is the source's stylistic framing, not a strict rule.
Format performance varies substantially by category — fashion, for example, does not typically run VSLs.

cards.title: Don't turn off evergreen campaigns for Black Friday — overlay them instead
cards.summary: Evergreen campaigns carry campaign-level conversion history, so turning them off resets learnings; overlay the Black Friday offer onto duplicates instead.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to pause evergreen campaigns during Black Friday and how to incorporate sale messaging into existing winners.
steps: Source: evergreen campaigns should hold ~50–60% of spend during Black Friday — the portfolio observed this share last year.
Duplicate your best-performing evergreen ads (including fatigued winners from a year ago) and badge them with the Black Friday offer.
Do not turn off the original evergreen ads when you run the overlayed version — the source says this is the single biggest mistake people make during Black Friday.

If you edit copy on evergreen ads to be Black Friday-specific, weigh the pros (more bottom-of-funnel messaging) against the cons (resetting the learning phase). The source treats this as a per-account decision, not a rule.
Ensure DPA catalog copy includes the sale messaging — the source cites a poll where 74% of cold brands had no written messaging in their catalog and only 3% included sale messaging.
Avoid pausing and restarting evergreen campaigns, which disrupts optimization learning.
caveats: The 50–60% of budget figure comes from the source's portfolio, not a universal rule.
Learning-phase behavior changes with platform updates — verify current treatment before making large changes.
Some ad platforms penalize significant-editing of live ads; the source acknowledges the trade-off rather than giving a clean answer.

cards.title: Distinguish creative quality from offer and product effects during Black Friday
cards.summary: Because the offer is doing so much work during Black Friday, ROAS during this period cannot reliably tell you whether a creative is good.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Black Friday ad performance and trying to decide which creatives to retire or scale.
steps: Recognize the confound: a 50%-off best seller will show a great ROAS even with mediocre creative; a strong scroll-stopping ad on a full-price, slow-moving product may show poor ROAS.
During Black Friday, do not treat top-ROAS ads as automatically the best creative. Use creative metrics (CTR, CPC, scroll-stop rate) to diagnose quality instead of ROAS.

Where practical, judge creative at the ad set level rather than the ad level, because multi-touch optimization plus last-click attribution plus Meta's breakdown effect makes ad-level ROAS unreliable during this period.
This flips normal practice — the source notes that in evergreen periods it would be wrong to judge ads on CPC alone; Black Friday is the exception because ROAS becomes noisy.
Use this diagnostic framing in your post-Black Friday retro to decide which concepts to carry forward, rather than blindly cutting the lowest ROAS ads.
caveats: The source is explicit that this is a Black Friday-period exception — it does not endorse CPC-based creative judgment year-round.
CPA/CPC thresholds themselves may shift with auction dynamics; compare within the same period.
Ideal approach is holdout-based incrementality, but that is often impractical for individual creatives.

cards.title: Scrape competitor Black Friday pages and ads for next year's planning
cards.summary: November is a strong scraping period because everyone is publishing their landing pages, offers and ads simultaneously — use it to build next year's data set.
cards.use_when: Running competitive research during Black Friday week to inform next year's Black Friday strategy for your store.
steps: Scrape competitors' Black Friday landing pages, offers, and ad creative during November while they're all live.
Record the number of distinct creative concepts each brand is running, not just total ad volume.

Source observation from a November scrape of fashion brands: higher-performing fashion brands ran more distinct core concepts (True Classic ~11, Ridge ~10, Threadheads ~9, Alo ~7, Gymshark ~6), while lower-performance-marketing peers ran fewer.

Note the counterexample: Skims shipped 429 unique visuals but only three core concepts — the source argues this is not advisable at large scale because you need concept breadth, not just visual volume.
Store the scraped set for next year's retrospective and creative planning, alongside your own account data.
Use it to sharpen your own concept count target — the source's takeaway is that diversity of concepts is what matters, not diversity of formats.
caveats: Brand names and concept counts are examples from one scrape of the source's fashion portfolio — not benchmarks for your category.
Scraping methodology and platform access change; verify what's permissible under platform terms before scraping.
Not all fashion brands follow the concept-volume pattern; the source itself flags Skims as an exception.

cards.title: Design Black Friday statics for one-second offer legibility and brand recognition
cards.summary: There is no single correct Black Friday aesthetic — a static succeeds if the offer is legible in under a second and the brand still looks like itself.
cards.use_when: Producing Black Friday ad statics or PDP hero assets where you need the offer and the brand to be instantly clear.
steps: Test against two criteria: (1) can a viewer understand the offer in under one second, and (2) do they still recognize the brand despite the discount context?
Keep the offer simple — 'up to X% off' style statements that are clear at a glance.
Keep product and logo identifiable; the source uses examples where the discount is clear and the brand logo remains visible.
Check legibility at thumbnail size during production, and check that feed placements don't crop the offer (9:16 layouts).
Put the offer and deadline in the first line of ad copy, since it truncates on story and some feed placements.
Apply the same legibility test to your PDP and landing page hero — the source frames legibility in under a second as the core requirement, which transfers to store surfaces.
caveats: The one-second legibility criterion is a design principle from the source, not a tested conversion benchmark.
Brand aesthetic norms differ substantially by category — a distinctive 'common format' in one brand's category may look out of place elsewhere.
